screens.title: Performance Metrics and the Iron Law
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore the Iron Law — the compact equation that links program behavior to processor design. You will learn how instruction count, cycles per instruction, and clock cycle time together determine execution time. We will use concrete examples to compute execution time, break down CPI into base and stall components, and compare processors using real benchmark ideas. Understanding the Iron Law helps you reason about trade-offs. For instance, a higher clock can be offset by increased stalls; an ISA that needs more instructions can raise execution time even with a fast core. We will also review benchmark suites such as SPEC, Geekbench, and MLPerf to see how sustained performance differs from peak specs. By the end, you will have the mental models and calculation steps to compare processors fairly, ask the right measurement questions, and avoid the common trap of trusting clock frequency alone. Consider how you would test a claim that a new chip is “20 percent faster” — that claim must be translated into the Iron Law to be validated.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Performance Metrics and the Iron Law

A compact, practical framework for predicting and measuring program execution time. We use numbers, decompositions, and benchmark thinking so you can compare processors accurately.

In this lesson
Apply the Iron Law to compute execution time and compare processors.
Coming up
Decompose CPI, quantify stalls, and use benchmarks responsibly.
Hands-on
Calculate execution time for three processors and evaluate pipeline trade-offs.
Concept map
Quick links
Iron Law
Execution Time = Instruction Count × CPI × Clock Cycle Time
CPI Decomposition
Base CPI + stall cycles from branches, loads, and structures.
Benchmarks
SPEC, Geekbench, MLPerf show workload-driven results, not just specs.
Measurement
Use performance counters and careful methodology to measure IC and CPI.
Tip: Treat clock frequency as a spec, not a guarantee of real performance.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide practical skills you will use when analyzing processor performance. First, you will apply the Iron Law to compute execution time for a program on a given processor. That means taking instruction count, CPI, and clock cycle time and producing a concrete time value; we will practice with numerical examples so you can validate performance claims. Second, you will compute CPI, IPC, and MIPS from processor specs and workload profiles. You will learn how CPI decomposes into base cycles and stall cycles caused by branches, loads, or structural hazards, and how to translate those numbers into IPC and MIPS where appropriate. Third, you will understand how clock frequency and pipeline depth interact: increasing frequency can reduce cycle time but can raise hazards and CPI. We will contrast cases where higher frequency helps vs. when it harms real execution time. Fourth, you will use benchmark thinking: SPEC, Geekbench, and MLPerf are tools to evaluate sustained workload performance rather than peak theoretical numbers. You will learn why benchmarks are necessary and how to interpret them critically.

screens.title: The Iron Law: execution time formula
screens.narratorSegment: The Iron Law is the central analytic tool: execution time equals instruction count times cycles per instruction times clock cycle time. In plain terms, execution time is driven by how many instructions a program issues, how many cycles those instructions take on average, and how long each cycle lasts. This equation is powerful because it isolates three levers an architect can change: reduce instruction count with a better ISA or compiler, reduce CPI by improving pipeline and caches, or reduce cycle time by raising clock frequency or simplifying the critical path. A concrete example: a program with 10 billion instructions, a CPI of 1.3, and a 2.5 nanosecond cycle time has execution time equal to 10e9 × 1.3 × 2.5e-9, which yields 32.5 seconds. A common misconception is to treat clock frequency alone as the measure of speed; frequency is only one factor and can be offset by higher CPI or more instructions. Ask yourself: which lever is cheapest to change for your workload — compiler improvements, microarchitecture, or process speed? That question guides meaningful optimizations and fair comparisons. The Iron Law: execution time formula means execution time = instruction count × cpi × clock cycle time — change any factor to affect runtime.. In practical terms, define and use the fundamental performance equation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Formula
keyIdea.text: Execution Time = Instruction Count × CPI × Clock Cycle Time — change any factor to affect runtime.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Iron Law
Definition and meaning

The Iron Law isolates the three independent contributors to execution time. Each term is measurable and often the target of microarchitectural change.

Equation
Execution Time = Instruction Count × CPI × Clock Cycle Time
Why this helps
It lets you predict the impact of compiler, microarchitecture, and process changes independently.
Common misconception
Clock frequency alone does not guarantee faster execution; CPI and instruction count can negate frequency gains.
Concrete example
# Example calculation
Instruction Count = 10,000,000,000
CPI = 1.3
Clock cycle time = 2.5e-9 seconds (400 MHz is 2.5e-9?)
Execution Time = 10e9 * 1.3 * 2.5e-9 = 32.5 seconds
Note: Use consistent units. Clock cycle time is the reciprocal of frequency. If frequency is quoted, convert to seconds per cycle before multiplying.
Key Takeaway

Treat execution time as a product of three measurable levers — optimize where the largest contributor lies.

screens.title: Instruction Count (IC)
screens.narratorSegment: Instruction Count is the total number of instructions executed by a program. It depends on three broad factors: the instruction set architecture, the compiler and its optimizations, and the algorithm used. For example, a complex instruction might implement several operations in one instruction on one ISA but require multiple simple instructions on another ISA; similarly, a better compiler can reduce redundant operations or use registers more effectively to lower IC. Measuring IC is practical: use hardware performance counters when available or run an instruction-set simulator that reports dynamic instruction counts. A common pitfall is assuming that fewer instructions always means faster code; if the remaining instructions are more expensive in CPI or cause more cache misses, execution time can increase. Consider a vectorized algorithm that reduces IC but increases memory traffic — the resulting CPI_stalls might dominate. End by asking: when you optimize for IC, what secondary effects will you measure to ensure overall execution time drops? Instruction Count (IC) means isa, compiler quality, and algorithm choice jointly determine dynamic instruction count.. In practical terms, what determines how many instructions a program runs?. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Instruction Count
What changes IC?
  • ISA: Some ISAs express work in fewer instructions.
  • Compiler: Optimization level, inlining, and register allocation affect counts.
  • Algorithm: Different algorithms perform different numbers of operations.
Measure IC
Use performance counters or simulators; ensure representative inputs and warm-up runs.
Concrete scenario
Imagine two compilers for the same ISA. Compiler A produces 1.2× more instructions than Compiler B on a workload. If CPI and cycle time stay constant, execution time increases proportionally to IC. But if Compiler B's instruction stream harms instruction locality and raises cache misses, the CPI_stalls may offset the IC savings.
Misconception
Fewer instructions doesn't guarantee faster runs unless you check CPI and memory behavior.
Pro tip
When optimizing IC, run performance counters to confirm reduced cycles and stalls.
Key Takeaway

Instruction count is necessary but not sufficient; always measure downstream effects on CPI and memory stalls.

screens.title: CPI and its decomposition
screens.narratorSegment: Cycles per instruction, or CPI, is an average metric that captures how many clock cycles each instruction consumes. We decompose CPI into a base CPI, representing the ideal pipeline throughput without stalls, and CPI_stalls, the sum of penalties from branches, load misses, and structural hazards. Formally: CPI = CPI_base + CPI_stalls, and CPI_stalls = CPI_branch + CPI_load + CPI_structural +.... Decomposition helps you see where cycles are lost. For example, suppose CPI_base is 1.0, 20 percent of instructions are branches with a 5 percent misprediction rate and a 10-cycle penalty. That branch penalty contributes 0.20 × 0.05 × 10 = 0.1 to CPI. Similarly, load misses can add more cycles depending on miss rate and penalty. A useful process is to list each instruction class, measure its frequency and effective penalty, and sum the contributions. A common mistake is to average only across retired instructions without attributing stall cycles to their causes; correct attribution reveals the most effective optimization targets. How would you change the pipeline or cache hierarchy if load stalls dominate CPI? CPI and its decomposition means break cpi into base and stall components to target the most costly hazards.. In practical terms, from base cpi to stalls caused by branches, loads, and structures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decomposition
keyIdea.text: Break CPI into base and stall components to target the most costly hazards.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › CPI Decomposition
Formal decomposition
CPI = CPI_base + CPI_stalls
CPI_stalls = CPI_branch + CPI_load + CPI_structural + ...
Measure each component by estimating the fraction of instructions in a class, the misprediction or miss rate, and the penalty in cycles. Multiply and sum to get the stall contribution.
Branch penalty
Contribution = fraction_of_branches × mispredict_rate × penalty_cycles
Load penalty
Contribution = fraction_of_loads × miss_rate × memory_penalty
Worked example
CPI_base = 1.0
Branches = 20% of instr, mispredict = 5%, penalty = 10 cycles
CPI_branch = 0.20 * 0.05 * 10 = 0.1
Loads = 25% of instr, miss = 4%, penalty = 20 cycles
CPI_load = 0.25 * 0.04 * 20 = 0.2
CPI_total = 1.0 + 0.1 + 0.2 = 1.3
Misconception: Not all stalls are permanent; some are amortized over instruction windows. Attribution still helps prioritize fixes.

screens.title: Computing CPI contributions
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a numeric CPI calculation step by step. We will compute the three parts shown earlier and confirm the total CPI. Start by listing instruction-class frequencies and their penalty behaviors. In our example CPI_base is 1.0. For branches: if 20 percent of instructions are branches, a 5 percent mispredict rate and a 10-cycle mispredict penalty multiply to a branch CPI of 0.1. For loads: 25 percent are loads with a 4 percent miss rate and a 20-cycle miss penalty, giving 0.2. Add these to get CPI = 1.3. Converting CPI into IPC is straightforward: IPC equals the peak issue width divided by CPI for single-threaded steady-state throughput assumptions, but keep in mind IPC is workload dependent. A mistake learners make is forgetting to convert percentages to fractions or mis-applying the penalty units; always ensure penalty cycles are in cycles and rates are fractions. To check your math, plug numbers back into the Iron Law to predict execution time and compare with measured runs — differences point to measurement error or omitted stall sources. Computing CPI contributions means list frequencies, convert rates to fractions, multiply by penalty cycles, and sum to find cpi_stalls.. In practical terms, step-by-step numeric calculation of cpi components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Numeric steps
keyIdea.text: List frequencies, convert rates to fractions, multiply by penalty cycles, and sum to find CPI_stalls.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › CPI Calculation
Step-by-step calculation
# Given
CPI_base = 1.0
Branches: fraction = 0.20, mispredict = 0.05, penalty = 10 cycles
Loads: fraction = 0.25, miss = 0.04, penalty = 20 cycles

# Compute contributions
CPI_branch = 0.20 * 0.05 * 10 = 0.1
CPI_load   = 0.25 * 0.04 * 20 = 0.2

CPI_total = CPI_base + CPI_branch + CPI_load = 1.0 + 0.1 + 0.2 = 1.3
After computing CPI, convert to IPC where useful, but remain aware that IPC depends on instruction-level parallelism and issue width assumptions.
Check your units
Percentages must be fractions; penalties are cycles. A common error is treating percentages as cycles directly.
Misconception
IPC is not an absolute property of a core; it depends on the workload mix and available parallelism.

screens.title: Clock Cycle Time vs. Frequency
screens.narratorSegment: Clock cycle time is the duration of a single clock tick; frequency is its reciprocal. Architects often speak in frequency because it is familiar, but you must convert frequency to cycle time to use the Iron Law. High frequency reduces cycle time, which can lower execution time for the same instruction count and CPI. However, achieving higher frequencies often requires deeper pipelines or more aggressive circuit design, which can increase CPI through hazards and penalties. A useful way to think about trade-offs is to compare two processors with different frequencies and CPIs. If frequency rises by 20 percent but CPI also rises by 25 percent, the net effect could be slower execution. A misconception is to treat frequency as additive performance; it multiplies with CPI in the denominator when converting execution time, so its impact depends on the other two factors. When estimating benefit, always compute execution time using consistent units to see whether frequency wins or loses in practice. Clock Cycle Time vs. Frequency means frequency helps only if resulting cpi and instruction count do not increase enough to offset cycle time reductions.. In practical terms, how cycle time relates to frequency and performance trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off
keyIdea.text: Frequency helps only if resulting CPI and instruction count do not increase enough to offset cycle time reductions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Frequency vs Cycle Time
Definitions
Clock cycle time = 1 / frequency. Use seconds per cycle as the unit when computing execution time. Higher frequency reduces cycle time but may raise CPI.
Example
2.5 GHz → cycle time = 1 / 2.5e9 = 0.4 nanoseconds. Use that in the Iron Law.
Misconception
Advertised GHz is not a direct measure of application speed without CPI and IC context.
Quick comparison table
Compare hypothetical changes by computing execution time for fixed IC:
# Processor X: freq=2.5 GHz, CPI=1.2
cycle_time = 1/2.5e9 = 0.4e-9 s
ExecTime_X = IC * 1.2 * 0.4e-9

# Processor Y: freq=3.0 GHz, CPI=1.5
cycle_time = 1/3.0e9 = 0.333...e-9 s
ExecTime_Y = IC * 1.5 * 0.333...e-9
# Compare ExecTime_Y / ExecTime_X to see net effect
Always compute the ratio to decide which processor is faster for your IC and CPI values.

screens.title: Pipeline depth, hazards, and performance
screens.narratorSegment: Deeper pipelines let a core run at higher clock frequencies by shortening the work per stage. However, more stages increase the window for hazards: branch mispredictions cause longer flush penalties in cycles, and inter-stage dependencies can raise stall rates. For example, doubling pipeline depth might allow a 50 percent frequency increase, but if it increases CPI by 30 percent due to larger misprediction costs and pipeline bubbles, the net execution time can worsen. The important lesson is that pipeline depth is an engineering trade-off: it buys frequency but can cost CPI. When evaluating pipeline changes, measure both the frequency gain and the change in CPI components, especially branch and structural penalties. In practice, architects mitigate hazards with better branch prediction, speculative execution, and forwarding, but these techniques add complexity and power cost. Ask: for your workload, do branch mispredictions or cache misses dominate? If branches dominate, deeper pipelines need better predictors to be beneficial. Pipeline depth, hazards, and performance means deeper pipelines can increase frequency but often raise penalties for mispredictions and hazards, potentially harming execution time.. In practical terms, why deeper pipelines can increase cpi despite higher frequency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Pipeline Depth
Why depth matters
  • More stages = shorter work per stage → higher possible frequency.
  • More stages = longer flushes and larger window for hazards → higher CPI penalties.
  • Mitigations like prediction and forwarding help but add complexity and power cost.
Design question
Is the workload branch- or memory-dominated? That answer guides whether deeper pipelines will help.
Scenario
Processor A doubles pipeline stages and raises frequency by 50% but sees CPI increase by 30%. Use the Iron Law to compute net effect for your workload. This is the canonical trade-off architects analyze numerically.
Pro tip: Pair pipeline depth changes with improved predictors to reduce the CPI impact of mispredictions.

screens.title: Benchmarks: SPEC, Geekbench, MLPerf, STREAM, CoreMark
screens.narratorSegment: Benchmarks are how architects and buyers translate design into workload performance. SPEC C P U offers SPECint and SPECfp to measure integer and floating-point C P U-bound workloads; Geekbench targets cross-platform single-core and multi-core responsiveness; MLPerf addresses machine-learning training and inference; STREAM measures memory bandwidth; CoreMark focuses on embedded C P U performance. The critical point is that each suite reflects different workload characteristics. You should select a benchmark that represents your application's behavior rather than trusting a single aggregate number. For example, a machine-learning workload that is heavy on matrix multiplies will be better represented by MLPerf than SPECint. Benchmarks also require strict methodology: same inputs, warm-up, versions, and isolated hardware. Vendors often advertise best-case benchmark numbers, so compare results on the same suite and configuration. A common pitfall is mixing benchmark types or failing to normalize for system differences such as memory capacity and input and output. Always ask which benchmark best models your actual workload before making design or procurement decisions. Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Benchmarks
Popular suites
  • SPEC CPU: CPU-bound integer and floating workloads.
  • Geekbench: Cross-platform single- and multi-core tests.
  • MLPerf: Machine learning training and inference measurement.
  • STREAM: Memory bandwidth tests.

Practical tip
Run the benchmark that matches your dominant workload and verify configuration details before trusting scores.
Interpreting scores
Benchmark scores are comparisons to references or normalized baselines. Look for single-core vs multi-core differences and whether the workload is memory- or CPU-bound. Vendors may optimize for a specific suite; real-world performance can diverge.

screens.title: Performance counters and measurement methodology
screens.narratorSegment: Measuring instruction count and CPI reliably requires a disciplined methodology. Use hardware performance counters when available to record retired instructions, cycles, cache misses, and branch mispredictions. When counters are absent or insufficient, instruction-set simulators can provide detailed dynamic counts. Key steps are: choose representative inputs, perform warm-up runs to stabilize caches and branch predictors, run multiple trials and take medians or means, and isolate the system to reduce interference from OS tasks and input and output. Also record configuration details: compiler flags, microcode versions, and power settings, because they affect reproducibility. A common error is running a single measurement and reporting it as definitive. Instead, report an ensemble of runs and confidence in results. When breaking CPI into components, attribute stall cycles to their sources using counter correlations, then use those contributions in the Iron Law calculation. That way, measurements become evidence for design decisions rather than anecdotal numbers. Performance counters and measurement methodology means use counters or simulators, warm-up runs, repeated trials, and full configuration logs to produce reliable performance numbers.. In practical terms, how to measure ic and cpi reliably in the lab. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: Use counters or simulators, warm-up runs, repeated trials, and full configuration logs to produce reliable performance numbers.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Measurement Methodology
Practical steps
  1. Select representative input datasets and execution modes.
  2. Warm up caches and predictors, then run trials.
  3. Collect counters for instructions, cycles, misses, and mispredictions.
  4. Repeat runs and report median or mean with variance.
Pitfall
Ignoring system noise and configuration differences leads to misleading comparisons.
From counters to CPI
Use counters to estimate fraction and penalty terms for CPI decomposition. For example, measure branch mispredictions and cycles lost to infer CPI_branch.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE: Produce a reproducible measurement script and report for one benchmark in the chosen suite.

screens.title: Compare three processors — execution time race
screens.narratorSegment: Now we apply the Iron Law to a hands-on comparison. Given a program with 10 billion instructions, compute the execution time on three processors. Processor A: 2 GHz, CPI 1.5. Processor B: 3 GHz, CPI 2.0. Processor C: 2.5 GHz, CPI 1.2. Convert frequencies to cycle time: cycle_time = 1 / frequency. Then compute execution time = IC × CPI × cycle_time. For A: cycle time = 0.5e-9 seconds, Exec_A = 10e9 × 1.5 × 0.5e-9 = 7.5 seconds. For B: cycle time = 0.333... e-9, Exec_B = 10e9 × 2.0 × 0.333... e-9 ≈ 6.67 seconds. For C: cycle time = 0.4e-9, Exec_C = 10e9 × 1.2 × 0.4e-9 = 4.8 seconds. So Processor C is fastest and A is slower than B in this example. Next, consider B's pipeline change: if frequency increases by 50% (to 4.5 GHz) but CPI increases by 30% (to 2.6), compute the new Exec and compare. These computations show how you must plug numeric changes into the Iron Law to decide if a design change is beneficial. Compare three processors — execution time race means compute cycle time from frequency and multiply by ic and cpi for direct execution time comparisons.. keyIdea.title: Hands-on
keyIdea.text: Compute cycle time from frequency and multiply by IC and CPI for direct execution time comparisons.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Hands-on: Race
Problem statement
Calculate execution time for IC = 10,000,000,000 on three processors.
# Given
IC = 10e9

Processor A: freq=2.0e9 Hz, CPI=1.5
cycle_A = 1/2.0e9 = 0.5e-9 s
Exec_A = IC * 1.5 * 0.5e-9 = 7.5 s

Processor B: freq=3.0e9 Hz, CPI=2.0
cycle_B = 1/3.0e9 ≈ 0.333333e-9 s
Exec_B = IC * 2.0 * 0.333333e-9 ≈ 6.67 s

Processor C: freq=2.5e9 Hz, CPI=1.2
cycle_C = 1/2.5e9 = 0.4e-9 s
Exec_C = IC * 1.2 * 0.4e-9 = 4.8 s
Result
Processor C is fastest (4.8 s), Processor A is slowest (7.5 s), B is intermediate.
Follow-up
If B increases frequency by 50% but CPI rises by 30%, recompute to decide whether performance improved.

screens.title: Assessment example: frequency claim analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Here is the classic assessment: a vendor claims a new processor is 20 percent faster because frequency increased from 2.5 GHz to 3.0 GHz, but CPI rose from 1.2 to 1.5 due to a deeper pipeline. We use the Iron Law. Execution time is proportional to CPI divided by frequency for fixed instruction count. Old execution time proportional to 1.2 / 2.5 = 0.48. New proportional time is 1.5 / 3.0 = 0.50. The ratio new/old is 0.50 / 0.48 ≈ 1.0417, meaning the new processor is about 4 percent slower, not 20 percent faster. This shows why frequency advertising can mislead. When you see a frequency increase claim, always ask how CPI changed and perform this simple ratio check. A common error is to ignore CPI or assume instruction count and CPI stay constant. The right question is: for my workload, does the CPI increase offset the frequency gain? If yes, then the advertised frequency advantage is not meaningful. Assessment example: frequency claim analysis means translate clock and cpi changes into execution time ratios to validate vendor performance claims.. In practical terms, evaluate a vendor claim using the iron law. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Assessment method
keyIdea.text: Translate clock and CPI changes into execution time ratios to validate vendor performance claims.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Vendor Claim Analysis
Question
Is the new processor faster when frequency increases but CPI also increases?
# Old: freq_old = 2.5 GHz, CPI_old = 1.2
time_prop_old = CPI_old / freq_old = 1.2 / 2.5 = 0.48

# New: freq_new = 3.0 GHz, CPI_new = 1.5
time_prop_new = CPI_new / freq_new = 1.5 / 3.0 = 0.50

# Ratio
ratio = time_prop_new / time_prop_old = 0.50 / 0.48 ≈ 1.0417
# New is ≈4% slower
Interpretation
The advertised GHz increase did not yield a faster processor because CPI grew enough to offset the benefit.

screens.title: Peak vs. sustained performance and the real-world gap
screens.narratorSegment: Peak performance numbers such as maximum IPC or peak FLOPS are useful for upper bounds, but sustained performance is what users experience. The gap between theoretical and actual performance arises from instruction mix, memory system limits, branch behavior, and software inefficiencies. For example, a core might sustain its peak FLOPS on a tightly vectorized kernel but deliver far lower performance on an irregular, memory-bound workload. Benchmarks attempt to capture sustained performance for classes of workloads. Measurement counters reveal where the gap originates — cache miss rates, pipeline stalls, and bandwidth ceilings. When optimizing, target the true bottleneck: if memory bandwidth limits sustained performance, improving cache latency or adding cores may not help. A common misinterpretation is to treat peak specs as normally achievable; instead, use workload-driven measures and report both peak and sustained numbers to give a complete picture. The practical step is always to profile, decompose with counters, and map fixes to the dominant stall contributor. Peak vs. sustained performance and the real-world gap means sustained performance depends on workload behavior; peak specs are only an upper bound and often unreachable for real applications.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Real-world gap
keyIdea.text: Sustained performance depends on workload behavior; peak specs are only an upper bound and often unreachable for real applications.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Peak vs Sustained
Sources of the gap
  • Instruction mix: not all code uses peak functional units.
  • Memory and bandwidth limits cause stalls regardless of peak compute.
  • Branch and pipeline behavior reduce sustained throughput.
Practical advice
Report both peak and benchmarked sustained numbers and document workloads and configuration.
Real-world connection
A server optimized for ML training will look different from one tuned for single-threaded latency. Benchmarks reveal the differences so architects can match hardware to workloads.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: To summarize, keep three ideas front and center. First, the Iron Law binds instruction count, CPI, and cycle time into execution time; use it to translate design changes into runtime consequences. Second, decompose CPI into base CPI and stall contributors like branch and load penalties so you can prioritize optimizations that actually reduce cycles. Third, rely on workload-driven benchmarks and disciplined measurement: frequency and peak specs are insufficient without CPI and instruction-count context. When testing a claim, convert frequencies into cycle times, compute execution time with measured CPI and IC, and compare ratios. Always report methodology details so results are reproducible. These habits let you spot misleading advertising and make sound architectural decisions based on measured impact rather than promise. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore the Iron Law — the compact equation that links program behavior to processor design. You will learn how instruction count, cycles per instruction, and clock cycle time together determine execution time. We will use concrete examples to compute execution time, break down CPI into base and stall components, and compare processors using real benchmark ideas. Understanding the Iron Law helps you reason about trade-offs. For instance, a higher clock can be offset by increased stalls; an ISA that needs more instructions can raise execution time even with a fast core. We will also review benchmark suites such as SPEC, Geekbench, and MLPerf to see how sustained performance differs from peak specs. By the end, you will have the mental models and calculation steps to compare processors fairly, ask the right measurement questions, and avoid the common trap of trusting clock frequency alone. Consider how you would test a claim that a new chip is “20 percent faster” — that claim must be translated into the Iron Law to be validated.

These objectives guide practical skills you will use when analyzing processor performance. First, you will apply the Iron Law to compute execution time for a program on a given processor. That means taking instruction count, CPI, and clock cycle time and producing a concrete time value; we will practice with numerical examples so you can validate performance claims. Second, you will compute CPI, IPC, and MIPS from processor specs and workload profiles. You will learn how CPI decomposes into base cycles and stall cycles caused by branches, loads, or structural hazards, and how to translate those numbers into IPC and MIPS where appropriate. Third, you will understand how clock frequency and pipeline depth interact: increasing frequency can reduce cycle time but can raise hazards and CPI. We will contrast cases where higher frequency helps vs. when it harms real execution time. Fourth, you will use benchmark thinking: SPEC, Geekbench, and MLPerf are tools to evaluate sustained workload performance rather than peak theoretical numbers. You will learn why benchmarks are necessary and how to interpret them critically.

These second-page objectives sharpen measurement and interpretation skills. You will learn to decompose CPI into base CPI and specific stall contributors: branch penalties, load misses, and structural hazards. That decomposition helps you target optimizations and quantify their impact on execution time. Next, you will learn how to measure instruction count and CPI in practice using performance counters or instruction set simulators, and why methodology matters: warm-up runs, consistent inputs, and isolating hardware sources of variation. Then, we will explore peak versus sustained performance and the gap that appears when caches, memory bandwidth, or software limit real throughput. Finally, you will practice translating benchmark reports into action: choose the right suite for your workload, understand normalization, and avoid comparing incompatible scores. These skills are essential when a vendor advertises clock speed but you need to know real-world execution time under your workload.

The Iron Law is the central analytic tool: execution time equals instruction count times cycles per instruction times clock cycle time. In plain terms, execution time is driven by how many instructions a program issues, how many cycles those instructions take on average, and how long each cycle lasts. This equation is powerful because it isolates three levers an architect can change: reduce instruction count with a better ISA or compiler, reduce CPI by improving pipeline and caches, or reduce cycle time by raising clock frequency or simplifying the critical path. A concrete example: a program with 10 billion instructions, a CPI of 1.3, and a 2.5 nanosecond cycle time has execution time equal to 10e9 × 1.3 × 2.5e-9, which yields 32.5 seconds. A common misconception is to treat clock frequency alone as the measure of speed; frequency is only one factor and can be offset by higher CPI or more instructions. Ask yourself: which lever is cheapest to change for your workload — compiler improvements, microarchitecture, or process speed? That question guides meaningful optimizations and fair comparisons. The Iron Law: execution time formula means execution time = instruction count × cpi × clock cycle time — change any factor to affect runtime.. In practical terms, define and use the fundamental performance equation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Instruction Count is the total number of instructions executed by a program. It depends on three broad factors: the instruction set architecture, the compiler and its optimizations, and the algorithm used. For example, a complex instruction might implement several operations in one instruction on one ISA but require multiple simple instructions on another ISA; similarly, a better compiler can reduce redundant operations or use registers more effectively to lower IC. Measuring IC is practical: use hardware performance counters when available or run an instruction-set simulator that reports dynamic instruction counts. A common pitfall is assuming that fewer instructions always means faster code; if the remaining instructions are more expensive in CPI or cause more cache misses, execution time can increase. Consider a vectorized algorithm that reduces IC but increases memory traffic — the resulting CPI_stalls might dominate. End by asking: when you optimize for IC, what secondary effects will you measure to ensure overall execution time drops? Instruction Count (IC) means isa, compiler quality, and algorithm choice jointly determine dynamic instruction count.. In practical terms, what determines how many instructions a program runs?. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cycles per instruction, or CPI, is an average metric that captures how many clock cycles each instruction consumes. We decompose CPI into a base CPI, representing the ideal pipeline throughput without stalls, and CPI_stalls, the sum of penalties from branches, load misses, and structural hazards. Formally: CPI = CPI_base + CPI_stalls, and CPI_stalls = CPI_branch + CPI_load + CPI_structural +.... Decomposition helps you see where cycles are lost. For example, suppose CPI_base is 1.0, 20 percent of instructions are branches with a 5 percent misprediction rate and a 10-cycle penalty. That branch penalty contributes 0.20 × 0.05 × 10 = 0.1 to CPI. Similarly, load misses can add more cycles depending on miss rate and penalty. A useful process is to list each instruction class, measure its frequency and effective penalty, and sum the contributions. Clock cycle time is the duration of a single clock tick; frequency is its reciprocal. Architects often speak in frequency because it is familiar, but you must convert frequency to cycle time to use the Iron Law. High frequency reduces cycle time, which can lower execution time for the same instruction count and CPI. However, achieving higher frequencies often requires deeper pipelines or more aggressive circuit design, which can increase CPI through hazards and penalties. If frequency rises by 20 percent but CPI also rises by 25 percent, the net effect could be slower execution. Deeper pipelines let a core run at higher clock frequencies by shortening the work per stage. However, more stages increase the window for hazards: branch mispredictions cause longer flush penalties in cycles, and inter-stage dependencies can raise stall rates. For example, doubling pipeline depth might allow a 50 percent frequency increase, but if it increases CPI by 30 percent due to larger misprediction costs and pipeline bubbles, the net execution time can worsen. The important lesson is that pipeline depth is an engineering trade-off: it buys frequency but can cost CPI. When evaluating pipeline changes, measure both the frequency gain and the change in CPI components, especially branch and structural penalties. Peak performance numbers such as maximum IPC or peak FLOPS are useful for upper bounds, but sustained performance is what users experience. The gap between theoretical and actual performance arises from instruction mix, memory system limits, branch behavior, and software inefficiencies. For example, a core might sustain its peak FLOPS on a tightly vectorized kernel but deliver far lower performance on an irregular, memory-bound workload. Benchmarks attempt to capture sustained performance for classes of workloads. Measurement counters reveal where the gap originates — cache miss rates, pipeline stalls, and bandwidth ceilings. When optimizing, target the true bottleneck: if memory bandwidth limits sustained performance, improving cache latency or adding cores may not help. To summarize, keep three ideas front and center. First, the Iron Law binds instruction count, CPI, and cycle time into execution time; use it to translate design changes into runtime consequences. Second, decompose CPI into base CPI and stall contributors like branch and load penalties so you can prioritize optimizations that actually reduce cycles. Third, rely on workload-driven benchmarks and disciplined measurement: frequency and peak specs are insufficient without CPI and instruction-count context. When testing a claim, convert frequencies into cycle times, compute execution time with measured CPI and IC, and compare ratios. Always report methodology details so results are reproducible.
